description: Coke is coal baked with little air to drive off its volatile matter, leaving a strong, porous carbon fuel. In 1709 Abraham Darby fired his Coalbrookdale blast furnace in Shropshire with coke as charcoal grew costly. Earlier trials had faltered; his was Europe's first lasting success, permitting larger furnaces and much cheaper cast iron.

claims: Darby smelted iron with coke at Coalbrookdale in 1709
made cast iron cheap at scale
not the first attempt, but the first in Europe to operate successfully for more than a few years
charcoal becoming costly
larger furnaces

uncertainty: Coalbrookdale is often called the first coke-fired blast furnace; Grace's Guide calls that claim not strictly correct. Accounts differ on how Darby treated the coal. The wider spread of coke smelting in Britain took decades and is not dated here.

factCheck.notes: Corroborated: 1709, Coalbrookdale, coke from local coal, charcoal costs, first lasting European success, larger furnaces, cheaper cast iron. General knowledge, not corroborated by search: the definition of coke (coal heated with little air to remove volatiles).

description: Lead crystal is glass made heavy and brilliant with lead oxide. In 1674 George Ravenscroft patented a clear English glass meant to rival rock crystal; when early pieces clouded, a defect called crizzling, he added lead, a change dated between 1674 and 1676. The denser, more refractive glass suited cut tableware and, later, the flint elements of achromatic lenses.

claims: 1674 seven-year patent for glass resembling rock crystal
crizzling
lead added, giving denser, more refractive glass
lead glass dated 1676; formula perfected by 1681
Dollond's 1758 achromatic lens combined crown and flint glass

uncertainty: Whether Ravenscroft found the lead effect himself or learned it from Venetian practice is debated; the lead formula is dated 1674 (Britannica) or 1676 (Toledo Museum) and was refined by about 1681. Achromatic lenses were made before Dollond's 1758 patent (Chester Moor Hall).

description: Puddling turned brittle pig iron into tough wrought iron without charcoal. In a coal-fired reverberatory furnace, where flame rather than fuel touched the metal, workers stirred molten iron until air burned out its carbon; the iron was then shingled and passed through grooved rolls. Henry Cort patented the rolls in 1783 and puddling in 1784; Welsh ironmasters made them practical.

claims: 1783 grooved-roll patent
1784 puddling patent: stirring in a reverberatory furnace to oxidise carbon, giving wrought iron
made practical at Cyfarthfa, Merthyr Tydfil, late 1780s-1790s
Peter Onions's similar 1783 patent
origin of the rolling idea contested

uncertainty: Cort built on earlier work (Peter Onions patented a similar process in 1783), and a claim that he took the rolling idea from a Jamaican foundry is contested. Sources date full commercial use at Cyfarthfa from about 1786 to the 1790s; his process at first suited white rather than grey pig iron.

description: Hot blast means preheating the air blown into a blast furnace. James Beaumont Neilson, manager of the Glasgow gas works, patented the idea in 1828. Heating the air to about 300 degrees Fahrenheit cut coal per ton of iron by over a third in one reported case, allowed raw coal instead of coke, and made Scotland's blackband ironstone worth smelting.

claims: 1828 patent
about 300 F; 8.06 to 5.16 tons of coal per ton of iron
raw coal instead of coke
Botfield priority claim
Neilson manager at the Glasgow gas works
blackband ironstone usable; rapid adoption in west Scotland
significance for fuel economy

uncertainty: Thomas Botfield's patent of January 1828 gives him a historical claim; Neilson is credited partly because he won patent litigation (notably against the Bairds of Gartsherrie, 1843). Where Neilson's first trials took place (Wilsontown or Clyde Iron Works) is reported differently. Fuel savings varied by works.

factCheck.notes: All claims (definition, Neilson's post, 1828 patent, temperature and fuel figures, raw coal, blackband ironstone) matched search summaries; the fuel figure rests mainly on a Wikipedia summary consistent with the other results.

description: The Bessemer process made steel by blowing air through molten pig iron in a tilting vessel; burning out carbon and silicon released enough heat to keep the charge liquid without added fuel. Henry Bessemer described it at Cheltenham in August 1856, while William Kelly reached a similar idea independently in the United States. It made bulk steel far cheaper.

claims: Cheltenham, British Association, August 1856
air blown through molten pig iron removes impurities and heats the metal
Kelly's independent US work and 1857 patent

uncertainty: Kelly's priority is debated; he received a US patent in 1857, a year after Bessemer's English patent. Early Bessemer steel suffered where ores contained phosphorus (see basic_process). The day of the Cheltenham paper is given variously (11 or 24 August 1856).

factCheck.notes: Corroborated: Cheltenham August 1856, air blown through molten pig iron heating it, Kelly's independent work. General knowledge, not corroborated by search: the tilting vessel, silicon as a heat source, no added fuel, and the cost reduction of bulk steel.

description: Open-hearth steelmaking melted pig iron with scrap and ore in a shallow hearth heated by Carl Wilhelm Siemens's regenerative furnace, which used waste heat to preheat gas and air. Pierre-Émile Martin first made steel this way at Sireuil, France, in 1864-65. Slower than a converter, it let steelmakers sample and adjust each charge, and it consumed scrap.

claims: Siemens regenerative furnace preheating gas and air
Martins first made steel with it in 1864
rise from the late 1860s
Sireuil, 1865

uncertainty: Martin's first steel is dated 1864 (Britannica) or 1865 (other sources); credit was later shared between Siemens and Martin, hence 'Siemens-Martin'. The process spread from the late 1860s.

factCheck.notes: Corroborated: Siemens regenerative furnace, Martin at Sireuil, 1864-65 dating. General knowledge, not corroborated by search: shallow hearth, charge of pig iron with scrap and ore, slower than a converter, sampling and adjusting the charge.

description: Acid-lined converters could not remove phosphorus, which made steel brittle. Sidney Gilchrist Thomas and his cousin Percy Gilchrist, experimenting at Blaenavon in Wales, lined the converter with basic material such as lime, which drew phosphorus into the slag. Announced in 1878, the method opened phosphoric ores in Lorraine and elsewhere, and its slag was sold as fertiliser.

claims: Thomas and Gilchrist at Blaenavon
basic (lime) lining took phosphorus into slag
announced 1878, paper 1879
phosphoric ore deposits made usable; value on the Continent
growth of Lorraine steel
slag sold as fertiliser (Thomas meal)

uncertainty: The 1878 announcement drew little notice and the formal paper was read in May 1879. The process was later displaced by open-hearth and other methods and had disappeared by the mid-1960s.

description: Portland cement is made by burning limestone or chalk with clay into clinker and grinding it to a powder that hardens with water. Joseph Aspdin patented the name in 1824, after Portland stone, but his product was probably underburned. Firing at much higher temperatures, as Isaac Charles Johnson did around 1845-50, produced the stronger modern material.

product probably too lightly burned
William Aspdin and clinker
Johnson's prototype about 1850
Johnson fired chalk and clay at 1400-1500 C, c. 1845

uncertainty: Who made the first true portland cement is disputed between the Aspdins (Joseph's patent, William's clinker) and Johnson; Johnson's work is dated 1845 locally and about 1850 by Britannica.

description: Metallography studies the inner structure of metals. From 1863 to 1865 Henry Clifton Sorby of Sheffield polished and etched steel and examined it under reflected-light microscopes, revealing distinct constituents. By about 1900 Roberts-Austen and Bakhuis Roozeboom had drawn the iron-carbon diagram, explaining hardening and tempering that smiths had long practised without knowing why.

claims: Sorby's researches 1863-65: polished and etched specimens, reflected-light microscopy
Roberts-Austen's diagrams 1897 and 1899; Roozeboom's phase-rule diagram c. 1900

uncertainty: Sorby's results were fully published only in 1886-87, and others (Martens, Osmond, Le Chatelier) developed the field in parallel; Widmanstatten had etched meteoritic iron earlier. Some 1897 diagrams by others are also claimed to precede Roberts-Austen's.

description: Aluminium is abundant in rocks but bound tightly to oxygen, so the metal was long a costly rarity. In 1886 Charles Martin Hall in the United States and Paul Héroult in France independently found that alumina dissolved in molten cryolite could be split by electric current. With Karl Josef Bayer's cheaper alumina from bauxite (1888-89), prices fell steeply.

Bayer process 1889 (or 1888)
Hall's samples and patent application, 1886
price fell about 80 percent by 1890 versus 1854
Bayer's cheaper alumina began cheap aluminium

uncertainty: The Bayer process is dated 1888 or 1889; price figures differ by source and baseline. Earlier chemical routes (Deville, 1850s) had already made small amounts of aluminium.

description: Superalloys are nickel-based alloys that keep their strength when red-hot and under stress. Patents from 1929 showed that titanium and aluminium could form tiny strengthening particles in nickel-chromium. After a British government request in 1939, Mond Nickel tested over a thousand experimental alloys; Nimonic 80, introduced in 1941, became the standard turbine-blade alloy of British gas turbines.

titanium and aluminium form the strengthening gamma-prime precipitate
1939 government request; over 1,000 alloys; Nimonic 80 in 1941; standard rotor-blade alloy of British gas turbines

uncertainty: Accounts differ on which early Nimonic alloy first solved turbine-blade failures and on the date of the improved Nimonic 80A. Cobalt- and iron-based high-temperature alloys were developed in parallel, notably in the United States.

description: Composite materials embed strong fibres in a resin so that each covers the other's weakness. A US patent for making glass fibres with air jets was sought in 1933, and glass fibre was paired with new plastic resins from 1936. In 1963 Britain's Royal Aircraft Establishment developed strong carbon fibre, later used in airframes and turbine blades.

uncertainty: Owens-Corning's founding is dated 1935 or 1938. Carbon fibres were made earlier (Union Carbide 1958; rayon process 1960), and Japanese work on PAN-based fibre in the same period is also credited; the 1963 date marks high strength, not first fibre.

description: Nanoscale engineering works with structures roughly 1 to 100 nanometres across, where surface and quantum effects change how materials behave. The scanning tunnelling microscope, built at IBM Zurich in 1981, made single atoms visible; in 1989 IBM researchers moved xenon atoms to spell the company's initials. Fullerenes (1985) and carbon nanotubes (1991) followed as new carbon forms.

description: Asteroid mining is the proposed extraction of water, metals or other materials from asteroids, for use in space or on Earth. It has not yet been done. Robotic missions have returned only small samples, such as Japan's Hayabusa2 from asteroid Ryugu in 2020. Two firms founded to pursue it, Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries, were sold in 2018-19.

description: Materials science studies how a material's structure, from atoms to grains, governs its properties, and how processing changes that structure. It took shape as a discipline in the 1950s, when Northwestern University broadened metallurgy into a department renamed materials science in 1958-59. Recent programmes, such as the US Materials Genome Initiative (2011), pair computation with experiment.

uncertainty: Northwestern's claim to the first such department is its own; the renaming is dated 1958 or 1959. The field drew together metallurgy, ceramics, polymer science and solid-state physics in several countries at once.
